text: A raw fact table is built for flexibility — every grain, every column, every join path an analyst might ever need. A Power BI report needs almost none of that. Pointing a dashboard straight at the fact table means redoing the same joins and aggregations from scratch, every single time.

The fix is a reporting layer — a view built specifically for what Power BI needs, pre-aggregated to the grain a dashboard actually filters on. This one rolls a transaction-level fact table up to daily totals by region, in one clean, secure view.

An ordinary view can leak its definition and execution details to a curious user with access to the underlying tables. Secure hides the view's definition from anyone without privileges on it, and limits what the optimizer exposes. Anything meant as "you see the summary, not the raw rows" should default to secure.

Snowflake's materialized views physically store and auto-maintain their result — genuinely useful for an expensive aggregation queried constantly. But they only support a single underlying table, no joins, which rules them out for most fact-and-dimension reporting. When a join is unavoidable, the real pattern is a scheduled task that writes the join's result into a physical summary table instead.

Three levers matter most for BI query patterns specifically: clustering keys, so a large fact table prunes to the date range a dashboard actually filters on; result caching, which serves identical repeated queries at effectively zero cost; and a reporting warehouse sized for many small similar queries, not the big batch jobs an ELT warehouse handles.
Next lesson steps back from SQL entirely to look at the bigger picture: where Snowflake fits alongside Data Factory, dbt, Python, and Airflow in a real modern data stack.
